# Platform config (v1)

Schema for `.tera/platform/<name>.hcl` config files. Each decodes to `pkg/config.PlatformBlock` carrying deployment-wide platform toggles. A singleton kind: at most one `platform` block across the vault.

**One attribute of the block may NOT be authored here: `tool_dispatch`.** It is the tool-dispatch containment posture — `mode = "remote_only"` says this daemon executes no tool dispatch in its own sandbox — and ADR-122 D2 Amendment 2 ratified it onto the restart-only side under the trust-posture reason, because a vault edit that could turn it off would re-enable execution an operator deliberately disabled. D5 then puts a restart-only attribute in the kernel. So it is authored in the bootstrap-HCL kernel, a file here that declares it is **refused** with a diagnostic naming the kernel as its home, and the composer re-asserts the kernel's posture onto the composed configuration whatever this kind does — including when the vault adopts the kind and declares nothing, or withdraws it. Changing the posture is a configuration edit *and a restart*: an edit to it is classified restart-required, so a reload announces `config.restart_required` rather than reporting it applied. `docs/ops/tool-dispatch-posture-is-kernel-owned.md` is the repair for a vault that has one today.

**Everything else in the block is vault-authored and reloadable**, unchanged: `correspondence_retention`, `correspondence_telegram`, `correspondence_unsolicited_inbound`, `cache_generation_cap`, `git_mirror_store_cap`, `plugins_domain` and `attended_idle_days`. A `capability_policy` block is REFUSED BY NAME (ADR-136 D11): it restricted wildcard capability references in agent definitions, which went with the agent kind, and nothing consulted it after — delete it. A `knowledge_bases` block is REFUSED BY NAME too (ADR-150 D9): it capped a knowledge-base source's monthly spend, and the knowledge base was retired — delete it. A `tracked_checkout_store_cap` attribute is REFUSED BY NAME (PLAN-2026-10 knowledge-bases §9): it bounded the daemon's store of tracked-checkout trees, and the daemon process keeps none — each host's trees are held in its runner's store, bounded by `tracked_checkout_store_cap` in that runner's configuration — delete it. The cache cap is deployment disk policy (ADR-124 D4), not binding policy; unset takes a finite 16 GiB default. GET /api/v1/config reports it beside Work Order concurrency as separate facts. No finite aggregate planning figure is established: one Work Order can acquire multiple generations. The cap is not an in-flight ceiling.

`git_mirror_store_cap` is the other disk-policy attribute, and it is here for a reason of its own beyond the one it shares with the cache cap: ADR-128's local git object mirror store is **daemon-owned precisely so that no recipe can name it** (D7 — a persistent volume resolves by binding label, and a nameable store is a mountable one), which closes a confidentiality hole and also removes the `data_volume { size_limit }` the size would otherwise have sat on. A binding's whole choice is whether to use the donor at all — and since D9 it uses one unless it says `mirror = false`; how large the store may grow is the deployment's. Unset takes a finite 2 GB ceiling (D8). **This attribute bounds THIS daemon's store and no other.** Each executing host keeps its own, because the clone is performed by the machine that provisions the workspace, so a fleet host bounds its own with the `git_mirror_store_cap` attribute in its `runner.hcl` — a runner mounts no vault and holds no desired state (ADR-106 D1), so the fact about that machine's disk is declared on that machine and takes effect at its restart rather than on reload. `docs/ops/git-object-mirror.md` is the operator's page for sizing either one and for seeding a cold one.

`plugins_domain` is ADR-140 D15's deployment-level domain for plugin UIs: each plugin that serves a UI is its own origin, `<name>.<plugins_domain>`, and unset means `localhost`, so `<name>.localhost` works with no DNS. It is here because it is a fact about this deployment's DNS, which neither a plugin's manifest nor one installation knows. One installation can leave its subdomain for tera's own origin only by its own elevated `path_based_ui` opt-in.

`attended_idle_days` is ADR-179 D9 item 5's idle limit: an attended session with no view of its terminal attached for that many whole days is ended by the daemon's idle sweep as `work_order.interrupt` ends one, parking `paused:interrupted` with the code `idle_limit` and its session kept for a resume. Unset means no limit. It is here because how long a session nobody is watching may hold its host is a fact about this deployment, which no type's author knows.

`correspondence_unsolicited_inbound` names the principal an UNSOLICITED correspondence arrival is addressed to — an arrival from an enrolled, currently verified transport identity that is not a reply to anything (PRD-021 §4.4). Presence is enablement: with no block declared this deployment has no unsolicited-inbound recipient and every such arrival is refused, which is the behaviour a deployment already has. **It SELECTS and does not GRANT.** Naming a principal here says where unsolicited mail goes and confers no reach whatever; whether a given sender may address it is the separate, unchanged ADR-118 D7 decision — `publish` on `correspondence/inbound/<hex>`, authored in `role` and `role_binding` recipes — so BOTH declarations must exist. The value is carried verbatim: a principal is opaque, and an EMPTY one is refused by `tera validate` because it would encode to an empty segment that an MQTT-style grant such as `correspondence/inbound/#` matches. Editing the recipient re-points the route on the next reload and REMOVING the block leaves no recipient behind. The route additionally needs a carrier whose descriptor can tell a reply from a new message (`native-thread` or `token-in-body`); a `none` carrier reports nothing that distinguishes the two, so the route is unavailable on one as a declared limitation while its ANSWER path is unaffected. `docs/ops/correspondence-inbound-acceptance.md` is the operator's page.

## Example

A minimal `platform`: every required attribute, exactly one member of each closed union, and nothing optional beyond what the kind would otherwise render empty. It is generated from the same source these tables are, and the same bytes are run through `tera validate` by the ADR-087 D9 pattern-transfer test — so it cannot describe a shape the loader does not accept.

Cross-references name the other kinds' examples (`example-worker`, `example-tool`, …) because every kind's example is validated together with the rest, as one vault.

`.tera/platform/example-platform.hcl`:

```hcl
version = "v1"

platform {}
```

## Attributes

| Attribute | Type | Required | Default | Since | Constraints | Description |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `cache_generation_cap` | string | no | `16GiB` | — | — | Deployment-wide cap for one bounded-by-size cache generation (ADR-124 D4). Author in the vault platform singleton; edits and withdrawal hot-reload. Unset means a finite 16 GiB cap, never unbounded. This starting assumption clears D6's illustrative 11 GiB peak with about 45% headroom and greatly exceeds Context's measured ~260 MB Go cache; it is not a fleet measurement and must be revised from usage evidence. Zero is refused. Uses the data-volume size grammar: B/KB/MB/GB/TB, K/M/G/T and IEC KiB/MiB/GiB/TiB spellings are powers of 1024; 10GB, 10G and 10GiB are identical; bare numbers are bytes. Malformed sizes are refused at validate. GET /api/v1/config reports the effective cap and each worker's max_concurrent_workorders as separate facts. No finite aggregate planning figure is established: a Work Order can acquire multiple generations. This is provision-time retirement policy, not an instantaneous ceiling: in-flight growth can exceed the cap. |
| `git_mirror_store_cap` | string | no | `2GB` | — | — | Deployment-wide ceiling on the TOTAL size of the ADR-128 local git object mirror store (D8) — the daemon-owned donor a volume binding's mirror = true borrows objects from. Author in the vault platform singleton; edits and withdrawal hot-reload. Unset means a finite 2 GB ceiling, never unbounded. Zero is refused: zero is not a spelling of unbounded, and a store with no bound is a date rather than a ceiling. The figure is anchored on measurement rather than intuition — a full mirror of kottera/kottera packs to 133 MiB while carrying 604 refs against 113 live branches, so that pack is already the steady state of accumulated dead-branch objects rather than a clean snapshot. Err generous: erring tight spends the uplink the mirror exists to spare, since evicting a mirror costs a full re-fetch where a lost build cache costs only local CPU. It bounds the WHOLE STORE and not one mirror; the store holds one mirror per normalized remote URL (D6), and over the ceiling the daemon RECLAIMS BEFORE IT DISCARDS — the maintenance pass runs first and only a still-over store evicts the least-recently-used whole mirror, never one a clone is reading. IT IS A DEPLOYMENT SETTING BECAUSE IT HAS NOWHERE ELSE TO LIVE: the store is daemon-owned precisely so that no recipe can name it (D7, which is what stops a session mounting every repository this host has ever cloned), so there is no data_volume size_limit for its size to sit on and nothing on the binding to hang it from. Uses the data-volume size grammar: B/KB/MB/GB/TB, K/M/G/T and IEC KiB/MiB/GiB/TiB spellings are powers of 1024; 2GB, 2G and 2GiB are identical; bare numbers are bytes. Malformed sizes are refused at validate; one that reaches a RUNNING daemon anyway leaves the 2 GB default standing rather than un-bounding the store, and says so on a WARN. The store resolves this against the CURRENT snapshot on every provision, so an edit takes effect at the next one with no restart. Operator page: docs/ops/git-object-mirror.md. |
| `plugins_domain` | string | no | `localhost` | PLAN-2026-09 plugins Wave 6 | — | The domain each plugin that serves a UI is served under, as its own subdomain <name>.<plugins_domain> (ADR-140 D15): with plugins_domain = "example-apps.net", the plugin whiteboard is served at whiteboard.example-apps.net. UNSET MEANS localhost, so a single machine serves whiteboard.localhost with no DNS at all: *.localhost resolves to loopback by definition. A real deployment's golden path is a plugins_domain under a registrable domain of its own, not tera's (tera.example.com beside *.example-apps.net), with a wildcard DNS entry and a wildcard certificate for *.<plugins_domain>: a browser keys SameSite on the registrable domain, so a plugin page under tera's own is same-site to tera and is sent tera's session cookie, and tera config plan warns about that shape. It separates plugins from tera only. Whether plugins are same-site to each other depends on the value, as observed in Chrome 155: under a plugins_domain that is or sits under a registrable domain (example-apps.net, or round.test standing in for one) the siblings are same-site, so a request one plugin's page makes to another's states Sec-Fetch-Site: same-site and carries that plugin's SameSite=Lax session cookie, and the reverse proxy's origin check is what keeps one plugin's page from acting for a person on another's. Under the default localhost they are NOT: a browser treats each <name>.localhost as a site of its own, so the same request states Sec-Fetch-Site: cross-site and the session cookie is withheld (SchemefulSameSiteLax). The default therefore isolates siblings further, with the origin check behind it, and a registrable plugins_domain is the value that gives same-site siblings. Each plugin gets its own origin, and so its own session: tera's session cookie is host-only on tera's origin and never reaches a plugin's subdomain, so a plugin's script cannot use a person's tera session. That separation is the reason for the subdomain, and one installation can give it up only by opting in with path_based_ui on its plugin block, which the plan's review marks elevated. It is DEPLOYMENT-LEVEL: it is not per plugin and never in a manifest. A lower-case DNS name of dot-separated labels, each of letters, digits and -, neither starting nor ending with -; no scheme, port, path, wildcard, or leading or trailing dot, and not an IP address, since an address takes no subdomain. Malformed values are refused at validate. Vault-authored and hot-reloadable: an edit takes effect on the next request the reverse proxy serves, and a person signed in to a plugin at its old host signs in again at its new one. A deployment with no plugin that serves a UI reads it for nothing. |
| `attended_idle_days` | integer | no | — | PLAN-2026-10 attended-sessions Wave 7 | — | How many whole days an attended session may go with no view of its terminal attached before the daemon ends it (ADR-179 D9 item 5). UNSET MEANS NO LIMIT: a session runs until it ends itself, is concluded, interrupted or cancelled. Idle means no view attached, a local attach on a personal runner included, for that many days, measured from when the last view detached, or from the session's dispatch when no view has attached since; attach and detach are the only activity tera observes, because it never reads the terminal. A session with a view attached is never idle. The daemon's sweep looks about every 15 minutes, so a session is ended within that much after its limit. An idle session is ended as work_order.interrupt ends one: its Work Order parks paused:interrupted with the code idle_limit, its workspace and harness session are kept, and its attendee resumes it with work_order.guide deliver, or tera workorder conclude ends it. Ending a session never touches an off-tera item it took. A whole number of days from 1 to 36500; zero and negative values are refused at validate, because zero is not a spelling of no limit: omit the attribute instead. A deployment fact, not a type's: it applies to every attended session this daemon runs. Vault-authored and hot-reloadable: an edit takes effect at the sweep's next pass. |
| `tool_dispatch` | block | no | — | — | — | Where this daemon's tool dispatches may execute — the remote-only containment posture. AUTHORED IN THE BOOTSTRAP-HCL KERNEL AND NOWHERE ELSE (ADR-122 D2 Amendment 2, trust posture; D5): a .tera/platform/ recipe that declares this block is REFUSED, with the refusal naming the kernel as its home, and the composer re-asserts the kernel's posture onto the composed configuration whatever a vault platform file does. Changing it is a configuration edit AND A RESTART — the posture is read once at boot, and there is no kernel file watcher (ADR-122 D5 declines to add one), so a reload does not read the kernel at all: it neither applies a posture edit nor reports one pending. An edit to it is classified restart-required rather than hot-reloadable, so IF a configuration carrying one ever reaches the diff — an API push, a programmatic reload — it is announced as config.restart_required and rendered hot_reloadable: false rather than reported applied. It is kernel-owned because it is a containment control: a vault edit that could turn it off would re-enable execution an operator deliberately disabled. Every OTHER attribute of the platform block is vault-authored and hot-reloadable as before. |
| `correspondence_retention` | block | no | — | — | — | — |
| `correspondence_telegram` | block | no | — | — | — | — |
| `correspondence_unsolicited_inbound` | block | no | — | — | — | — |

## `tool_dispatch` block

| Attribute | Type | Required | Default | Since | Constraints | Description |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `mode` | string | no | `local` | PLAN-2026-08 §6 scope 9 | — | Where this daemon's tool dispatches may execute. AUTHORED IN THE BOOTSTRAP-HCL KERNEL AND NOWHERE ELSE, and changing it is a restart rather than a reload (ADR-122 D2 Amendment 2, trust posture; D5) — a .tera/platform/ recipe declaring tool_dispatch is refused. Accepted: "local" \| "remote_only". "local" (the default; unset means this) runs them in the daemon's own sandbox. "remote_only" says this daemon orchestrates and does not execute: a sandboxed tool dispatch that would have run here is refused naming the posture, whether or not a runner is connected — there is deliberately no fallback to local execution. It gates ONE seam: the sandboxed execution of a tool INVOCATION in this daemon's own process. "Invocation" rather than "spawn" is exact — the management API, the broker, triggers, the Work Order orchestrator, connectors, native (in-process) tool handlers, and the describe/materialize schema protocol that builds this daemon's tool catalog are all untouched in both modes. The MCP gateway is untouched only on its FAR side (upstream calls and the projected tools of an upstream, whose work happens on the far side already); a virtual server's locally-backed tool member is an ordinary local dispatch and IS refused. There is no per-capability exemption from this posture: local_capabilities was that and is RETIRED (ADR-133 D7/D15). A daemon that is both an orchestrator and a gateway declares mode = "local" here and narrows what this host offers with runner "local" { serves = [...] } in the vault — the permission is this attribute and needs a restart, the definition is that one and hot-reloads. Declaring a runner does not turn this on; nothing infers it. |
| `local_capabilities` | string[] | no | — | ADR-106 implementation note (#3826) | — | RETIRED (ADR-133 D7/D15) and REFUSED under every mode — declaring it is an error, not a no-op. It was the operator's exemption set: capabilities a remote_only daemon executed in its own sandbox ANYWAY, read by a gate underneath the placement. There is no longer a gate there. Containment is now structural, so a daemon that may not execute has no local runner to place work on, and an exemption beneath that has nothing to exempt from. The exemption set survives as a NARROWING of what this host offers — runner "local" { serves = [...] } — which takes TWO declarations where this took one: platform { tool_dispatch { mode = "local" } } in the bootstrap-HCL kernel is the PERMISSION and needs a RESTART (it is the containment decision, ADR-122 D2 Amendment 2), and runner "local" { serves = [...] } in the vault under .tera/runners/local.hcl is the DEFINITION and hot-reloads. This is deliberately NOT migrated: the first half rewrites a containment posture from remote_only to local, which only an operator may decide, and the second puts this host into the fleet as a member that draws a seat and is counted against its meters — which the exemption set never did. The capability names carry over verbatim; only the seam moved. If you meant this daemon to orchestrate and not execute, delete this attribute and change nothing else — remote_only with no local runner is that posture, and is now the whole of it. |

## `correspondence_retention` block

| Attribute | Type | Required | Default | Since | Constraints | Description |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `content_window` | string | no | — | — | — | How long a message's CONTENT is kept — body, response contract, the settling answer and its values — measured from the hub's own assignment stamp (ADR-117 D10's content clock). A Go duration string: 90 days is "2160h", because time.ParseDuration has no day unit. Unset takes the deployment_profile default, which is 90 days on every profile and is stated by PRD-021 §20 as a GUESS rather than a measurement — nothing has been measured, because no corpus of real correspondence exists to measure yet. Must be positive: a zero or negative window is not a posture, it is a cutoff at or after now that would collect every message the moment it was written, and it is refused offline by tera validate rather than enforced. A deadline is not a retention clock and this window is not one either way round: the sweep reads the assignment stamp and never the deadline, so a short deadline cannot shorten retention (ADR-117 D10). |
| `record_window` | string | no | — | — | — | How long a DELIVERY RECORD is kept — endpoint, transport class, rendering digest, degraded flag, attempts, and who answered and when — measured from the record's own recorded_at stamp (ADR-117 D10's record clock). A Go duration string: one year is "8760h". Unset takes the deployment_profile default, which is one year on every profile and is stated by PRD-021 §20 as a GUESS. Must be positive. MUST NOT BE SHORTER THAN THE CONTENT WINDOW: the whole of ADR-117 D10 is that records outlive the content they describe, so a shorter record window would collect the audit history while the bodies it describes survive — which makes PRD-021 SC7 unanswerable in exactly the case SC7 is about, and does it silently. Declaring both windows with this one shorter is refused offline by tera validate. Declaring only ONE of them cannot be refused offline, because the other comes from a profile default this validator cannot see; there the daemon HOLDS the record window at the content window's floor and warns on the boot line, so what is in force is not what was written. |

## `correspondence_telegram` block

| Attribute | Type | Required | Default | Since | Constraints | Description |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `bot_token` | string | yes | — | PLAN-2026-09 Wave 4 | — | Credential reference for the Telegram bot token issued by @BotFather — env://VAR, keychain://service, vault://path, secret://row, or literal://<value>. Re-resolved on EVERY delivery rather than read once at boot, so rotating the material behind the reference takes effect on the next message with no daemon restart, and so a deployment that configures a bot and never sends never reads the secret at all. Adding or removing this block does not need a restart either: the carrier is linked and unlinked on reload (ADR-122 D1). A BARE LITERAL is refused outside the dev and test profiles: this block is authored in a vault file (.tera/platform/<name>.hcl), a vault is a git tree, and a token written here is a credential committed to one and visible to everyone who can read the repository — the repair is to put it in the secret store and name it. literal://<value> is the escape hatch for an operator who means it, and warns on every profile. The token is never logged, never returned in an error, never placed on a receipt and never written to a delivery record; it is carried in the Bot API request path and nowhere else. That holds for a literal too: the daemon prints a REFERENCE on its boot line and in a delivery-record error, and a reference on a scheme it cannot resolve — a literal, or literal:// — is withheld rather than printed, because on those the reference IS the credential. |
| `api_base_url` | string | no | — | — | — | Base URL of the Bot API server. Unset means https://api.telegram.org, which is what nearly every deployment wants. It exists because the Bot API documents running the server locally ("Using a Local Bot API Server"), and it is the ONLY source of a host this carrier will contact — there is no fallback host and no second endpoint anywhere in the adapter. Must be an absolute https:// URL: the bot token travels in the REQUEST PATH rather than in a header, so a plaintext base would put the deployment's bot credential on the wire in a form every proxy and access log along the way records. http:// is refused offline by tera validate for that reason, including for a loopback address. |
| `api_ca_bundle` | string | no | — | PLAN-2026-09 Wave 4 | — | Credential reference for the PEM CA bundle that vouches for api_base_url's server — env://VAR, keychain://service, vault://path, secret://row, or literal://<pem>. Unset means the system trust store, which is what you want against Telegram's own host. It exists because api_base_url and the https rule together are not usable without it: a local Bot API server ("Using a Local Bot API Server") presents a certificate signed by whatever authority its operator runs, and there is no loopback exemption from https — so without a bundle that deployment works only if its server happens to hold a publicly chained certificate. It REPLACES the system trust store for Bot API calls rather than adding to it: the authorities that may vouch for your Bot API server are exactly the ones named here. That is why declaring it while api_base_url is Telegram's own host is refused rather than ignored — the system roots are what verify that host, and replacing them with a private bundle would break every call with a certificate error. Unlike bot_token this is not a secret: a CA certificate is public material, literal:// draws no warning, and the reference is printed on the boot line. Resolved on the first call that needs it rather than at boot, so a deployment that configures a bot and never sends still reads nothing (PRD-021 SC6). Editing this attribute is reloadable like the rest of the block — point it at a different reference and the next call uses it. Renewing the certificate IN PLACE under an unchanged reference is NOT picked up, unlike bot_token which is re-resolved per delivery: the bundle is read once and the transport built from it is held for the life of that configuration, so a renewal takes effect when the reference changes or the daemon restarts. |

## `correspondence_unsolicited_inbound` block

| Attribute | Type | Required | Default | Since | Constraints | Description |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `recipient` | string | yes | — | PLAN-2026-09 Wave 6 | — | The principal an UNSOLICITED correspondence arrival is addressed to on this deployment — an arrival from an enrolled, currently verified transport identity that is not a reply to anything (PRD-021 §4.4). Author it in the vault platform singleton; edits and withdrawal hot-reload with no restart, and a removed block leaves NO recipient behind. IT SELECTS AND DOES NOT GRANT: naming a principal here says where unsolicited mail goes and confers no reach whatever. Whether a given sender may address it is the separate, unchanged ADR-118 D7 decision — publish on correspondence/inbound/<hex>, authored in role and role_binding recipes — so BOTH declarations must exist: a recipient with no grant admits nothing, and a grant with no recipient has nothing to address. With no block declared every unsolicited arrival is refused, which is the behaviour a deployment already has; the refusal is the one constant SenderRefusal string, indistinguishable from unenrolled and from ungranted, with the daemon log naming that no recipient is declared. THE VALUE IS CARRIED VERBATIM: no case folding, no Unicode normalization, no prefix stripping and no truncation, because the bytes are the identity and nothing anywhere reads a principal's spelling (ADR-118 D2, PRD-021 SC10). An EMPTY principal is refused offline by tera validate on ErrEmptyPrincipal's own reasoning: an empty principal encodes to an empty segment, and correspondence/inbound/ is a topic-shaped string that an MQTT-style grant such as correspondence/inbound/# matches. The admitted message travels the ordinary record and send path — attention admission, retention, content class, delivery accounting — so a recipient with no live interactive window takes whatever road the deployment's configuration provides. Operator page: docs/ops/correspondence-inbound-acceptance.md. |
